title: Chemical Kinetics
tagline: Rate laws, mechanisms, collision and transition-state theory, chain reactions, catalysis, oscillations, surfaces, photochemistry and dynamics
summary: Kinetics asks how fast reactions go and by what path. This course turns rate measurements into rate laws and mechanisms, explains rates with collision and transition-state theory, and treats chain reactions, catalysis and oscillations, reactions at surfaces, photochemical kinetics and the dynamics of single reactive encounters.
overview: Thermodynamics tells us which reactions are possible; kinetics tells us what actually happens, and on what timescale. Diamond is metastable in air, yet the diamond in a ring lasts a human lifetime, while an explosion of hydrogen and oxygen is over in milliseconds. Chemical kinetics is the science of that span: how fast a reaction proceeds, how the rate depends on concentration and temperature, and what sequence of molecular events — the mechanism — produces the observed rate law.

The course begins where measurement does. Rates are measured by following concentration in time — spectrophotometrically, conductimetrically, by pressure — and from those curves we extract rate laws, rate constants and half-lives. We then learn that a rate law is evidence for a mechanism, not proof of one, and we build the machinery that connects mechanisms to rates: the steady-state approximation, the pre-equilibrium approximation, and the identification of rate-determining steps.

The middle of the course explains what the rate constant means. Collision theory counts molecular encounters; transition-state theory (Eyring) recasts the rate constant in terms of the free energy of the activated complex, so that activation enthalpies and entropies become measurable. From there we branch outward: radical chain reactions and combustion, homogeneous catalysis and oscillating reactions, adsorption and catalysis at surfaces, photochemical kinetics, and finally molecular beam experiments and reaction dynamics.

What makes kinetics hard is not the mathematics — mostly first-order differential equations and some statistical averaging — but the bookkeeping: many intermediates, several approximations in play at once, and the need to check that every derived rate law reproduces the observed orders. The remedy is the same throughout this atlas: derive every result yourself, check its limiting behaviour, and read the numbers of real experiments. By the end you should be able to take a published rate law and say what mechanism it supports, and what it cannot tell you.
outcomes: Measure reaction rates by following concentration in time — spectrophotometrically, conductimetrically, or by pressure — and convert a measured signal into a concentration–time record.
Derive the integrated rate laws for zero-, first- and second-order reactions, extract rate constants from linear plots, and compute half-lives.
Apply the method of initial rates and the isolation method to determine reaction orders experimentally.
Apply the steady-state and pre-equilibrium approximations to multi-step mechanisms and derive their composite rate laws.
Estimate collision frequencies and Arrhenius parameters, and explain steric factors and the temperature dependence of rate constants.
Use the Eyring equation to obtain enthalpies and entropies of activation, and interpret kinetic isotope effects.
Analyse chain reactions, catalytic cycles and oscillating reactions with the steady-state approximation, and explain explosion limits.
Derive the Langmuir and BET adsorption isotherms and distinguish Langmuir–Hinshelwood from Eley–Rideal surface kinetics.
Interpret Stern–Volmer quenching data, quantum yields and photochemical rate laws, and relate them to excited-state lifetimes.

chapters.title: Rate laws and their measurement
chapters.summary: Experimental methods for following reactions, initial rates and the isolation method, and integrated rate laws of zero, first and second order.

chapters.title: Reaction mechanisms
chapters.summary: Elementary steps and molecularity, consecutive and competing reactions, the steady-state approximation, pre-equilibria and rate-determining steps.

chapters.title: Collision theory
chapters.summary: Molecular collisions, the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of speeds, steric factors and the origin of the Arrhenius equation.

chapters.title: Transition-state theory
chapters.summary: The activated complex, the Eyring equation, enthalpies and entropies of activation, and kinetic isotope effects.

chapters.title: Chain reactions
chapters.summary: Radical chain mechanisms, the hydrogen–bromine reaction, chain branching and explosion limits.

chapters.title: Catalysis, autocatalysis and oscillating reactions
chapters.summary: Acid–base and homogeneous catalysis, catalytic cycles, autocatalysis, and oscillating reactions such as the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction.

chapters.title: Adsorption and reactions at surfaces
chapters.summary: Physisorption and chemisorption, the Langmuir and BET isotherms, and the Langmuir–Hinshelwood and Eley–Rideal mechanisms.

chapters.title: Photochemical kinetics
chapters.summary: Absorption and quantum yields, the rates of fluorescence, phosphorescence and energy transfer, and quenching and the Stern–Volmer equation.

chapters.title: Molecular reaction dynamics
chapters.summary: Potential energy surfaces, trajectories and molecular beams, and diffusion-controlled reactions in solution.

history.title: Wilhelmy formulates the law of active masses
history.detail: In his doctoral dissertation at Heidelberg, Wilhelm Wilhelmy showed that the rate of inversion of sucrose by acid is proportional to the concentration of sucrose, and that the catalyst is not consumed — the first quantitative rate law.

history.title: Guldberg and Waage publish the law of mass action
history.detail: Cato Maximilian Guldberg and Peter Waage, in a memoir to the Christiania Videnskabsselskab, proposed that chemical affinity is proportional to active mass, laying the foundation of both equilibrium and kinetics.

history.title: Arrhenius introduces the exponential temperature dependence
history.detail: Svante Arrhenius, studying the inversion of cane sugar by acids, found that rate constants grow exponentially with temperature and introduced the activation energy and the equation that carries his name.

history.title: Langmuir develops the theory of adsorption
history.detail: Irving Langmuir derived the isotherm for monolayer adsorption and showed that surface reactions follow the coverage of the adsorbed layer, founding surface kinetics — work recognised by the 1932 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

history.title: Eyring publishes transition-state theory
history.detail: Henry Eyring's paper 'The Activated Complex in Chemical Reactions' recast the rate constant as the flux of an activated complex in quasi-equilibrium with reactants; Evans and Polanyi arrived at the same idea independently.

history.title: Belousov discovers the oscillating reaction
history.detail: Boris Belousov found that the bromate–cerium citrate system oscillates in a well-stirred solution, a result rejected by journals for years and published only as a footnote in 1959.

history.title: Eigen receives the Nobel Prize for kinetic methods
history.detail: Manfred Eigen, Ronald Norrish and George Porter shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the study of extremely fast reactions — the relaxation method, flash photolysis and pulse radiolysis — which opened the microsecond and shorter timescale.

history.title: The Nobel Prize for reaction dynamics
history.detail: Dudley Herschbach and Yuan T. Lee shared half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the development of the crossed molecular beam method, which resolves individual reactive scattering events; Marcus Polanyi shared the other half for energy disposal in elementary reactions.

history.title: Femtochemistry makes the transition state observable
history.detail: Ahmed Zewail's Nobel Prize recognised femtosecond laser pulses that record molecular motion during the reaction itself, turning the transition state from an inference into something that can, in principle, be watched.
